Feature attribution methods — SHAP, integrated gradients, attention rollout, GradCAM variants — purport to answer "which input features caused this prediction?" The central question is whether attribution scores are a stable property of the model's decision function or merely an artifact of the specific input representation chosen. The instability emerges sharply when you apply semantically equivalent perturbations: synonym substitution in NLP, contrast normalization in vision, feature rescaling in tabular data — transformations that leave the ground-truth label and (usually) the model's output probability unchanged, yet systematically scramble the attribution map. A beginner sees this as a robustness nuisance; an expert recognizes it as a deeper epistemic crisis — if two encodings of the same semantic content produce attribution maps with low rank-order correlation, then the attribution is not measuring model reasoning, it is measuring the interaction between the model's internal geometry and the specific surface form of the input, which is a fundamentally different and far less useful quantity. The expert also worries about a subtler failure mode: because saliency methods are often used to build trust or flag spurious correlations, unstable attributions can generate false confidence — a practitioner might conclude a model relies on legitimate features when the attribution merely reflects whichever surface encoding happened to be passed in.

Integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017) integrates the gradient of the output with respect to the input embedding vector along a straight-line path from a baseline x' to the actual input x, accumulating how much each embedding dimension contributes to the output change across that interpolation. The attribution for token A is the dot product of this path-integrated gradient with the displacement vector (x − x'), so the score is jointly determined by gradient sensitivity and the geometric direction of the displacement in embedding space. The baseline choice is the first and most consequential instability source: the canonical zero-vector baseline places x' at a point that is typically off-manifold — it corresponds to no real token in the vocabulary — meaning the integration path traverses regions the model was never trained on, where gradients are essentially arbitrary. When you apply a semantically equivalent perturbation (swap "fast" → "rapid"), both the displacement vector and the integration path change, and because the embedding manifold is non-linear and anisotropic, the accumulated gradients along the two paths can diverge substantially even if the endpoint predictions are identical; Kindermans et al. (2019) in "The (Un)reliability of Saliency Methods" demonstrated exactly this class of failure, showing input-invariant transformations produce attribution changes that expose path-dependence rather than semantic content. A PAD-token or mask-token baseline (common in BERT-based attribution pipelines like those in the Captum library) partially mitigates off-manifold traversal but introduces a different bias: the baseline now carries its own semantic signal, so the attribution measures importance relative to the masked state, which means synonym substitution changes the baseline-relative geometry even when the model's functional behavior is unchanged.

Completeness means the attribution scores sum exactly to F(x) − F(x'), which is a accounting identity: every unit of output difference is allocated across input dimensions with no remainder. This is mathematically guaranteed by the fundamental theorem of calculus applied along the integration path, and it holds regardless of whether that path passes through coherent, in-distribution inputs — the integral converges to the correct value even when every intermediate interpolant x_α = x' + α(x − x') is a nonsensical embedding that no real token occupies. The critical confusion is that completeness is a constraint on how the budget is distributed, not on what the budget measures: if the integration path exits the data manifold immediately, the gradients being integrated reflect the model's behavior in an extrapolated, effectively arbitrary region, and the resulting allocation is a faithful accounting of a fictitious quantity. Adebayo et al. (2018) in "Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps" made this concrete by showing that saliency methods including IG produce visually similar and equally "complete" attributions even after randomly reinitializing the upper layers of a network — the completeness axiom was satisfied throughout, yet the attributions were demonstrably insensitive to the model's learned weights, which is the definition of semantic faithlessness. The deeper point is that axioms like completeness, sensitivity, and implementation invariance were derived from a desiderata list about mathematical consistency, not from any empirical theory of what makes a human-interpretable explanation reflect model reasoning; satisfying them is necessary but nowhere near sufficient for the attribution to track the causal structure the practitioner assumes it tracks. For semantic equivalence specifically, two inputs x and x_syn sharing the same F-value will have identical completeness budgets (both compute F(x) − F(x')), yet their attribution maps can have near-zero Spearman rank correlation because the displacement vectors and off-manifold gradient fields differ — the axiom is doubly satisfied and doubly uninformative.

Manifold-constrained paths sound appealing but immediately face a uniqueness problem: the geodesic between two points in a high-dimensional learned embedding space is not unique when the manifold has non-trivial curvature or topology, and in practice encoders like BERT or a ResNet's penultimate layer produce manifolds with both — meaning the "same" attribution computation can yield different results depending on which geodesic solver or manifold approximation you use. Computationally, geodesics are typically approximated via shortest paths through a neighborhood graph built over real data points (e.g., using k-NN graphs as in the Riemannian manifold IG variant proposed by Frye et al., 2020), which introduces a second instability: the attribution now depends on which data points happen to be in the neighborhood graph, making it sensitive to dataset composition in ways that have nothing to do with the model or the input. The semantic-equivalence problem can actually worsen because manifold paths route through semantically loaded intermediate points — real tokens, real sentences — so a path from "fast" to a baseline may pass through "quick," "rapid," or "speedy" depending on manifold geometry, while the path from the synonym "rapid" to the same baseline takes a different route through different neighbors, accumulating gradients over a completely different set of intermediate semantics. This means two synonymous inputs now produce attribution maps that differ not only because their displacement vectors differ (the original IG problem) but also because the gradient is integrated over different semantic neighborhoods, amplifying rather than canceling the instability. There is also a circularity problem: the manifold is defined by the encoder whose attributions you are trying to interpret, so any instability in the encoder's representation of semantic equivalence — which is precisely what causes the original attribution instability — is now baked directly into the integration path, providing no independent ground truth. Agarwal et al. (2021) in "Towards the Unification and Robustness of Perturbation and Gradient Based Explanations" showed empirically that path-constrained variants do not consistently outperform straight-line IG on faithfulness metrics, precisely because the path geometry introduces new degrees of freedom that trade one instability for another.

Perturbation-based methods estimate feature importance by marginalizing over a coalition distribution — SHAP computes a weighted average of the model's output across all subsets of features present or absent, and LIME fits a local linear surrogate to outputs sampled by randomly masking input regions. The structural vulnerability is that "absent" must be operationalized as a concrete replacement value, and for any non-trivial input modality this operationalization is itself a semantic choice: in NLP, masking token A means replacing it with [MASK], UNK, a sampled token from the marginal distribution, or zero-embedding, and each choice produces a different conditional distribution over the remaining features, a different local neighborhood, and therefore different Shapley values. This is categorically harder to fix than the IG baseline problem because in IG the baseline affects one interpolation endpoint, whereas in SHAP the "absent" operationalization affects every element of the 2^n coalition space — the instability is not localized to a single geometric choice but is distributed across an exponential number of marginalization decisions, each of which can interact with the others. Concretely, Chen et al. (2023) showed that switching NLP SHAP from [MASK]-token absence to marginal-sample absence changes token attribution rankings with Spearman ρ as low as 0.3 on BERT-based sentiment classifiers, on inputs where the model output is identical — the attribution instability is total while the predictive behavior is unchanged. For semantically equivalent inputs the problem compounds: synonym substitution changes which tokens are present in each coalition, altering the marginal statistics of the sampled absences, so the Shapley value of token A in sentence S₁ and the Shapley value of its synonym in S₂ are estimated against different implicit reference distributions even if F(S₁) ≈ F(S₂). LIME adds a further instability layer because the local linear fit depends on the sampling radius in input space, and semantically equivalent inputs that sit at slightly different positions in embedding space will induce different local neighborhoods, different surrogate fits, and different importance rankings — the locality hyperparameter is doing hidden semantic work that is never made explicit.

Several formulations attempt to sidestep the absence problem entirely by grounding attribution in the model's internal computations rather than input counterfactuals. Attention-based attribution (raw attention weights, attention rollout, or gradient-weighted attention) requires no baseline or masking — it reads importance directly from the model's learned routing weights — but Jain & Wallace (2019) and Wiegreffe & Pinter (2019) demonstrated that attention weights are not faithful to model outputs in the sense that you can often find alternative attention distributions producing identical predictions, meaning attention attribution is measuring a component of the forward pass, not causal importance. A more principled absence-free class is influence functions (Koh & Liang, 2017), which attribute prediction behavior to training data points by approximating how the model's parameters would shift if a training example were upweighted, using the inverse Hessian of the training loss — no input baseline required, attribution lives in training-data space rather than feature space. The new instability class these methods introduce is parametric sensitivity: influence functions depend on the curvature of the loss landscape via the Hessian inverse, which is computationally approximated (e.g., via LiSSA or EK-FAC), and Basu et al. (2021) showed that influence function estimates are highly unstable across random seeds, model checkpoints, and Hessian approximation methods — correlations between estimates from different runs can fall below 0.1 on identical models. A third absence-free approach is probing-based attribution, which trains auxiliary classifiers on intermediate representations to measure how much information about each feature is linearly decodable at each layer; this requires no baseline but introduces a new instability: the probe's own capacity and training dynamics determine what counts as "information," so attribution depends on the probe architecture as much as the model being explained. What unites these methods is that they trade baseline-dependence for structural dependence — on attention geometry, loss curvature, or probe expressivity — and these structural dependencies are equally sensitive to semantically equivalent input perturbations because the internal representations that drive them are themselves non-invariant to surface form changes.

When semantically equivalent test inputs x and x_syn produce divergent influence rankings, the immediate implication is that the model's representation function maps them to different neighborhoods in the training data manifold — the Hessian-weighted inner product ∇_θ F(x)ᵀ H⁻¹ ∇_θ F(x_train) that defines influence is sensitive to the exact gradient direction in parameter space, and synonym substitution rotates that gradient vector enough to change which training examples have the largest inner product. This reveals something precise about the learned representation: the model has not achieved semantic invariance in its parameter gradients even when it has achieved it in its output probabilities — F(x) ≈ F(x_syn) but ∇_θ F(x) ≇ ∇_θ F(x_syn), meaning the model arrived at the same output prediction via functionally different internal computations that are sensitive to different training signals. Geometrically, this means the training data manifold as seen through the model's gradient space is more finely grained than the manifold as seen through the model's output space — two test points that are output-equivalent are gradient-distinct, and their local curvature neighborhoods in parameter space (captured by H⁻¹) may overlap with entirely different clusters of training examples. Pruthi et al. (2020) in "Estimating Training Data Influence by Tracing Gradient Descent" made this concrete by showing that influence rankings are highly sensitive to which checkpoint in training you evaluate at, implying the gradient-space geometry is itself non-stationary — and if checkpoint timing changes rankings, synonym substitution, which produces a comparably small gradient rotation, certainly will. The deeper implication is that divergent influence rankings under semantic equivalence expose a representational gap: the model has learned a function that is semantically coarse at the output level but semantically fine-grained at the gradient level, and this mismatch means any attribution method that operates in gradient or parameter space will inherit a sensitivity to surface form that the output-level behavior does not predict or explain. This is arguably more troubling than feature-attribution instability because influence functions are often used to diagnose training data quality and detect spurious correlations — if the rankings are surface-form-dependent, a practitioner might incorrectly attribute a prediction to a training example that reinforced legitimate generalization when in fact the influence ranking merely reflects an accidental gradient alignment with a surface feature.

Contrastive fine-tuning with synonym pairs — as in SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021) or augmentation-based consistency training — explicitly minimizes the distance between h(x) and h(x_syn) in representation space, which does propagate some invariance backward through the network: if the final hidden states are aligned, the gradients of the output with respect to those hidden states will be more similar, partially collapsing the gradient-space fine-graining. However, the propagation is incomplete for a precise architectural reason: contrastive loss aligns representations at the layer where it is applied, but the gradient of the task loss with respect to parameters in earlier layers depends on the full chain rule through all subsequent layers, and those intermediate Jacobians are not directly constrained by the contrastive objective — meaning gradient-space geometry at early layers can remain fine-grained even when late-layer representations are aligned. Dong & Shutova (2021) examined BERT models fine-tuned with synonym augmentation and found that while cosine similarity between synonym representations improved substantially in layers 9–12, gradient similarities measured via influence function proxies remained low in layers 3–6, confirming the layer-wise decoupling between representation alignment and gradient alignment. A subtler issue is that contrastive fine-tuning can actually sharpen gradient-space discrimination in unintended ways: by pulling synonym representations together, it steepens the loss landscape in the directions orthogonal to the synonym axis, increasing gradient magnitude sensitivity to any residual surface-form differences that survive the alignment — the Hessian eigenspectrum becomes more anisotropic, not less. Data augmentation with synonym pairs during pre-training (as studied in BERT-aug variants) shows a similar pattern: output-space invariance improves on paraphrase benchmarks by 15–20% accuracy points, but influence function rank correlations between synonymous test inputs improve only marginally, suggesting the training-data manifold geometry in gradient space is restructured but not homogenized. The fundamental obstacle is that output-space invariance is a scalar constraint (F(x) ≈ F(x_syn)) while gradient-space invariance is a vector constraint (∇_θ F(x) ≈ ∇_θ F(x_syn)) with dimensionality equal to the parameter count — satisfying the scalar constraint is compatible with arbitrarily large gradient divergence in the null space of the output function, and no standard training objective directly penalizes that divergence.
